checks.title: Management group hierarchy, no subscription at the tenant root
remediation: Create a management group hierarchy: platform, landing zones, sandbox.
Move every subscription under it, so policy and role assignments inherit.

userImpact.text: An Azure structure only administrators see.

checks.narrative: A subscription at the tenant root inherits nothing: no benchmark, no policy, no standing-access rules. Management groups are where those are set once.

checks.title: Microsoft cloud security benchmark assigned on every subscription
checks.remediation: Enable Defender for Cloud on the listed subscriptions, or assign the benchmark initiative at the management group so new subscriptions inherit it.

userImpact.text: Recommendations appear for administrators; no user change.

checks.narrative: The benchmark is the policy set behind Azure Secure Score and every Defender for Cloud recommendation. A subscription without it is unevaluated, not clean.

checks.title: Defender for Cloud plans on where the resource types exist
checks.remediation: Turn on the Defender plan for each listed subscription and resource type: Servers, Storage, Key Vault, Databases, Containers, App Service, APIs, and Resource Manager everywhere.

userImpact.text: Protection runs in the background; no user change.

checks.narrative: The plans are the paid detections: runtime threat detection on VMs, malware scanning on storage, anomalous Key Vault access. Off on a subscription that holds the resource is the finding; off elsewhere is fine and noted.

checks.title: Defender CSPM enabled
checks.remediation: Enable Defender CSPM on the subscriptions where attack paths, permissions creep and unused-permission findings are wanted.

userImpact.text: Attack path findings appear for administrators only; no user change.

checks.narrative: Defender CSPM adds attack path analysis and the identity findings Entra Permissions Management used to carry. Without it those rows are not evaluated.

checks.title: Security contact with alert notifications on every subscription
checks.remediation: Set a security contact email on each listed subscription with alert notifications for high severity and above, and the Owner role notified.

userImpact.text: Alert emails go to the security contact; no user change.

checks.narrative: Defender for Cloud alerts that nobody is emailed about sit in the portal. The contact is who finds out.

checks.title: Activity log exported from every subscription
checks.remediation: Add a diagnostic setting on each listed subscription that sends the activity log categories to the Log Analytics workspace or Sentinel, with a year or more of retention there.

userImpact.text: Logging users never see.

checks.narrative: The activity log holds every control-plane change and is kept 90 days on its own. The export is what makes an investigation older than that possible.

checks.title: Delete locks on Key Vaults and Recovery Services vaults
checks.remediation: Apply a CanNotDelete lock to each listed vault, or to its resource group.

userImpact.text: Administrators must remove the lock before deleting a vault.

checks.narrative: A Key Vault or backup vault deleted by mistake, or by an attacker with Contributor, is the outage and the ransomware scenario in one. The lock is cheap.

checks.title: Policy coverage beyond the benchmark on every subscription
checks.remediation: Assign the organisation's own policies (deny public IPs, deny public storage, require encryption, allowed locations) at the management group.

userImpact.text: Engineers who deploy resources may have non-compliant deployments refused.

checks.narrative: The benchmark audits. The organisation's own deny policies are what stop a misconfiguration from being created at all.

checks.title: Owner and environment tags on the fleet
remediation: Enforce the owner and environment tags with a policy that inherits them from the resource group.
Tag the resource groups.

userImpact.text: Engineers who deploy resources are asked for owner and environment tags.

checks.narrative: A resource with no owner tag is a resource nobody will answer for when the finding lands. Tags are the join key between the posture report and the people.

checks.title: No orphaned resources
checks.remediation: Delete the unattached disks, unused public IPs, NICs without a VM and empty resource groups, or document why each stays.

userImpact.text: Removing unused resources changes nothing anyone uses.

checks.narrative: Orphans cost money and carry data: an unattached disk still holds the VM's contents. The counts are the clean-up list.

checks.title: Owners per subscription within the limit, none synced from AD
checks.remediation: Reduce standing Owners to three or fewer named cloud-only accounts per subscription; everyone else gets Contributor or an eligible PIM assignment.

userImpact.text: People who lose Owner work as Contributor or activate Owner in PIM.

checks.narrative: Owner on a subscription is full control including the right to grant it. Owners inherited from the root or a management group count too; synced accounts tie the subscription's fate to on-premises AD.

checks.title: No standing Owner or User Access Administrator at root or management group
checks.remediation: Remove the standing assignments at the root and management group scopes and make them eligible through PIM for Azure resources.

userImpact.text: Administrators activate root and management group roles in PIM when needed.

checks.narrative: A permanent Owner at the root scope owns every subscription that exists and every one created later. Eligible is the only acceptable state for that role.

checks.title: No guest users with Azure role assignments
checks.remediation: Remove the guest assignments, or record each as an object-level exception with the partner and the reason.

userImpact.text: Guests lose their Azure access unless it is recorded as an exception.

checks.narrative: A guest with an Azure role is a partner's account, governed by the partner's MFA and lifecycle, with rights in your subscription.

checks.title: Service principals with Owner or Contributor justified
remediation: Record each service principal listed as an exception with its purpose.
Prefer a managed identity over an app secret.
Scope it to a resource group rather than the subscription.

userImpact.text: Workloads keep running; their identities get narrower scope.

checks.narrative: A service principal with Contributor is a credential that can rebuild the subscription. Pipelines need it; the question is which ones and at what scope.

checks.title: No orphaned role assignments
checks.remediation: Delete the assignments whose principal no longer exists.

userImpact.text: Removing assignments to deleted principals changes nothing.

checks.narrative: An assignment to a deleted principal is noise now and a grant to whoever recreates the object id later. They accumulate with every leaver.

checks.title: No custom roles with wildcard actions
checks.remediation: Rewrite the listed custom roles with explicit actions; a role that grants * is Owner with a different name.

userImpact.text: People with the rewritten role may lose actions they did not need.

checks.narrative: Wildcard actions in a custom role defeat the point of the custom role and hide an Owner-equivalent grant from every review that looks for Owner.

checks.title: No classic administrators
checks.remediation: Remove the listed Co-Administrators and Service Administrators; the role type was retired in 2024 and anything left is unmanaged access.

userImpact.text: Former classic administrators lose that access and use an Azure role instead.

checks.narrative: Classic administrators sit outside RBAC and PIM. Microsoft retired the type; a tenant that still has them has access nobody reviews.

checks.title: Role assignments to individual users at resource scope within the limit
checks.remediation: Replace per-user assignments on individual resources with group assignments at resource group scope; the count is the trend to drive down.

userImpact.text: People keep their access through groups instead of direct assignments.

checks.narrative: Hundreds of per-user grants on individual resources are unreviewable. Groups at resource group scope are the maintainable shape.

checks.title: Key Vaults on the RBAC model with purge protection, soft delete and no public access
remediation: Switch each vault listed to RBAC authorisation, checking which identities used access policies first.
Enable purge protection and soft delete.
Disable public network access or set the firewall default to deny.

userImpact.text: Apps that reach a vault over the internet, or through access policies, need a private endpoint or a role first.

checks.narrative: Key Vault holds the secrets everything else depends on. Access policies are the legacy model nobody reviews; purge protection is what stops an attacker deleting the keys for good.

checks.title: Storage accounts without shared keys, anonymous blobs or HTTP
remediation: Move the clients of each account listed to Entra authentication, or SAS tokens that are scoped and dated.
Disable shared key access and anonymous blob access.
Require HTTPS and TLS 1.2.

userImpact.text: Apps that use storage keys, anonymous access or plain HTTP fail until moved to Entra sign-in or scoped tokens.

checks.narrative: A storage account key is a password to every byte in the account, and anonymous blob access is the classic public-bucket leak. Both are off by one switch each.

checks.title: Azure SQL servers on Entra-only authentication
checks.remediation: Enable Entra-only authentication on each listed SQL server once the applications use managed identities or Entra logins.

userImpact.text: Apps that sign in to SQL with a username and password fail until moved to a managed identity or Entra login.

checks.narrative: SQL authentication is a password in a connection string. Entra-only removes it as a path, the same move as disabling shared keys on storage.

checks.title: Conditional Access covers the Azure management plane
checks.remediation: Create a Conditional Access policy that targets Windows Azure Service Management API (Microsoft Azure Management) for all users and requires MFA or a phishing-resistant strength and a compliant device.

userImpact.text: Administrators answer MFA when they use the Azure portal, CLI or PowerShell.

checks.narrative: The portal, CLI and ARM API are all the management plane. A policy on all cloud apps covers it; a tenant with app-specific policies often leaves it out.

checks.title: Microsoft 365 pay-as-you-go spend has a budget alert
remediation: On each subscription listed, create a budget in Cost Management with alerts at 80 and 100 percent to the people who own Microsoft 365.
Limit Owner and Contributor on the paying subscription; anyone with them can change the billing policy (AZ-011).

userImpact.text: Nothing visible; the owners hear about spend before the invoice.

checks.narrative: Microsoft 365 pay-as-you-go services (Backup, Archive, SharePoint Premium, Copilot messages) bill to an Azure subscription with no cap; a budget only alerts, but without one the first sign of runaway usage is the invoice.

checks.title: No management ports open to the internet
remediation: Remove or narrow each rule listed: allow SSH, RDP and WinRM only from known addresses, or not at all.
Reach virtual machines through Azure Bastion or just-in-time VM access in Defender for Cloud instead of open ports.
Add an Azure Policy that denies network security group rules allowing these ports from the internet, so new ones cannot appear.

userImpact.text: Administrators connect through Azure Bastion or a just-in-time request instead of a port open to the world; nobody else notices.

checks.narrative: Remote desktop, SSH and WinRM open to the whole internet are found by scanners within minutes and then guessed at around the clock; exposed RDP remains one of the most common ways into an organisation for ransomware crews. A rule on a network security group in use is all it takes.

checks.title: A budget with an alert on every subscription
remediation: In Cost Management, Budgets, create a monthly budget for each subscription listed, near its normal spend, with alerts at 80 and 100 percent to the owner and the operations mailbox.

userImpact.text: No one notices until spend jumps, and then the owner hears about it the same day instead of on the invoice.

checks.narrative: A sudden jump in Azure spend is often the first visible sign of a compromised subscription: crypto-mining, mass virtual machine creation or abused AI services. A budget alert turns that into a message the same day rather than a surprise on next month's invoice.

checks.title: Backup vaults keep deleted backups and refuse to shorten them
remediation: In each vault listed, Properties, Security settings, set soft delete to Always on (or at least enabled with 14 days or more).
Turn on immutability, and lock it once the retention settings are settled, so backups cannot be shortened or deleted early even by an administrator.
Keep multi-user authorization (Resource Guard) in mind for the vaults that hold the most critical backups.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for people; backups simply cannot be deleted or shortened by mistake or by an attacker.

checks.narrative: Ransomware operators go for the backups first: deleting recovery points, or shortening retention so they expire, before they encrypt anything. Soft delete keeps deleted backups recoverable for days, and an immutable vault refuses the change altogether, so the restore is still there when it is needed.

checks.title: Microsoft Sentinel receives Entra, Microsoft 365 and Defender XDR
remediation: In the Sentinel workspace, Content hub, install the Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Defender XDR solutions and connect their data connectors.
For Entra ID, send at least sign-in and audit logs; for Defender XDR, connect incidents and alerts.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for people; the security team sees identity, mail and endpoint activity in one place.

checks.narrative: A Sentinel workspace without the Microsoft 365 sources sees little of what attackers do in a Microsoft 365 tenant: no sign-ins, no mailbox activity, no Defender alerts. These three connectors are free to ingest for the most part and carry the evidence most investigations start from.

checks.title: Entra Domain Services without legacy protocols
remediation: In the managed domain's Security settings, turn off NTLM v1 authentication, TLS 1.2 only (TLS 1.0 off) and Kerberos RC4 encryption.
Turn off password synchronisation from on-premises NTLM hashes unless an on-premises app still needs NTLM, and turn on Kerberos armoring, LDAP signing and channel binding.

userImpact.text: Old devices or apps that still use NTLMv1, TLS 1.0 or RC4 against the managed domain stop working; test with them first.

checks.narrative: Entra Domain Services gives legacy apps a domain to join and ships with old protocols on for compatibility. NTLMv1 and RC4 make captured credentials easy to crack or relay, and TLS 1.0 is long broken; most managed domains no longer need any of them.

checks.title: Azure Policy compliance at or above the threshold
remediation: Open Azure Policy, Compliance, and start with the assignments listed here: they are the ones most resources break.
For each, fix the resources (many built-in policies offer a remediation task) or, where the policy does not fit a workload, record an exemption on that scope with a reason and an end date.
Move policies that are only audited to deny or deploy-if-not-exists once the estate is clean, so new resources cannot break them.

userImpact.text: Fixing a resource to meet a policy can change how it is reached or logged; each policy says what it changes.

checks.narrative: Assigning a policy says what the rules are; compliance says whether the estate follows them. This is the share of the resources Azure Policy has evaluated that break no assigned policy, across the subscriptions that were read, with the assignments most resources break. A low figure with the benchmark assigned usually means the benchmark was assigned and never worked.

checks.title: Azure Lighthouse delegations with more than read access justified
remediation: For each delegation listed, confirm the partner still works for you and still needs that role on that scope.
Remove a delegation that is no longer wanted: Azure portal, Service providers, Delegations, then remove it.
Ask the partner to republish an offer that is too broad with narrower roles, or with eligible (just in time) access for the roles that change things.
Record the delegations that stay as exceptions with an owner and a review date.

userImpact.text: None for your users. A partner whose delegation is removed loses access at once, so agree it with them first.

checks.narrative: Azure Lighthouse lets people in another organisation's tenant act on your subscriptions with a role you granted once, when an offer was accepted. Their accounts, their MFA and their leavers are theirs to manage, not yours, and the delegation stays until someone removes it. A delegation that only reads is left alone. One with Contributor or any other role that can change things, or one whose roles could not be read, is listed so that each has a name next to it.
